Title: Duplicate invoice submission is allowed for the same PO and invoice number
Steps to Reproduce: 1. Log in as a registered vendor (e.g., vendor@testcorp.com). 2. Navigate to Invoice Submission. 3. Select PO number: PO-2026-045. 4. Enter invoice number: INV-TC-001. 5. Enter invoice date: 10 May 2026. 6. Enter invoice amount: $5,000.00. 7. Upload a valid PDF attachment. 8. Click Submit. 9. Observe the success confirmation. 10. Without logging out, navigate back to Invoice Submission. 11. Repeat steps 3–8 with the exact same PO number, invoice number, amount, and date. 12. Click Submit again.
Expected Result: The system should detect the duplicate submission based on the combination of (vendor ID + PO number + invoice number) and display an error: 'An invoice with this number already exists for PO-2026-045. Please review your submission.' No second invoice record should be created.
Actual Result: The second submission is accepted without any warning or error. Two separate invoice records are created for the same PO with the same invoice number, amount, and date. Both appear in the AP team's review queue with different invoice IDs (e.g., invoice/501 and invoice/502).
Impact: Critical financial risk. If both invoices are approved — even accidentally — the vendor would receive a double payment for the same work. In high-volume periods, duplicate invoices in the AP queue increase the risk of erroneous approval due to workload.
Suggested Fix: Implement server-side duplicate detection before persisting the invoice record. Validate that no existing record matches the combination of (vendor_id + po_number + invoice_number). If a match is found, return a 409 Conflict response with a clear user-facing error message.

Title: Rejected invoice is incorrectly forwarded to payment processing
Steps to Reproduce: 1. Log in as a registered vendor. 2. Submit a valid invoice against PO-2026-067 (Invoice number: INV-TC-002, Amount: $12,500.00). 3. Log out and log in as an AP team member. 4. Open the submitted invoice (INV-TC-002) from the queue. 5. Click Reject. 6. Enter rejection reason: 'Invoice amount does not match the agreed PO terms'. 7. Confirm the rejection. 8. Verify the invoice status in the portal — it shows Rejected. 9. Check the payment processing queue (downstream system or payment table in DB).
Expected Result: The invoice status should be Rejected. No record for INV-TC-002 should appear in the payment processing queue. A rejection notification should be sent to the vendor.
Actual Result: Despite the invoice showing Rejected status in the portal, a payment record for INV-TC-002 with the amount of $12,500.00 is found in the payment processing queue. The payment system has been triggered as if the invoice was approved.
Impact: Critical business and financial defect. If not caught before payment run, the vendor would be paid for an invoice that was explicitly rejected by the AP team. This indicates a race condition or incorrect conditional logic in the payment forwarding trigger.
Root Cause Hypothesis: The payment forwarding event appears to be triggered by an invoice status change event generically, rather than specifically checking for status = Approved. The rejection flow updates the status but may emit the same event type as an approval, or the approval event fires before the transaction completes.
Suggested Fix: Review the payment forwarding logic to ensure it is triggered only when invoice.status == 'Approved'. Add an explicit condition check before emitting the payment event. Consider adding an integration test that verifies the payment queue remains empty after a rejection action.

Title: Vendor can access another vendor's invoice by modifying the invoice ID in the URL
Steps to Reproduce: 1. Log in as Vendor A (vendorA@testcorp.com). 2. Navigate to My Invoices. 3. Open an invoice and note the URL pattern: https://portal.example.com/invoices/501. 4. Note that Vendor B has an invoice with ID 502 (obtained from another vendor account during testing). 5. Modify the URL to: https://portal.example.com/invoices/502. 6. Observe the page that loads.
Expected Result: Access to invoice/502 (owned by Vendor B) should be denied for Vendor A. System should return a 403 Forbidden response or redirect Vendor A to their own dashboard with a message: 'You do not have permission to view this invoice.' No data from Vendor B's invoice should be displayed.
Actual Result: The page loads successfully and displays Vendor B's invoice in full detail, including: Vendor B's company name and registered email, PO reference number, invoice amount ($8,200.00), invoice attachment (PDF is viewable/downloadable), and approval status and reviewer comments. Vendor A has full read access to Vendor B's confidential financial documents.
Impact: Serious data privacy and security defect (IDOR — Insecure Direct Object Reference). In a B2B financial application, exposing one vendor's invoice data to another vendor is a contractual and potentially regulatory violation. Vendors can view competitors' pricing, PO values, and business relationships.
Root Cause Hypothesis: The invoice detail API endpoint (GET /invoices/{id}) is not validating that the authenticated user's vendor_id matches the vendor_id on the requested invoice. The endpoint returns the record based solely on the invoice ID without ownership verification.
Suggested Fix: Add a server-side ownership check on the GET /invoices/{id} endpoint. After fetching the invoice record, verify that invoice.vendor_id == authenticated_user.vendor_id. If they do not match, return a 403 Forbidden response. This check must also be applied to any invoice-related endpoints (update, download attachment, etc.). Do not rely on UI-level hiding alone.
